reading.title: Closing Perspective — Extend the System Without Losing the Argument
paragraphs: The progression from C++ syntax to distributed architecture is not a progression away from fundamentals. It makes ownership, lifetime, invariants, and evidence more important because each must now cross additional boundaries. A pointer can outlive an object; a callback can outlive a request; a retry can outlive a caller; a receipt can outlive the process that created it. Each lifetime needs an owner and a defined end.

The same is true of promises. A parser accepting bytes, a database committing intent, a worker recording an effect, and a client observing a result are different events. Reliable architecture connects them with recoverable state instead of collapsing them into one reassuring success flag.

HarborDispatch is deliberately limited so that this argument remains inspectable. Its value is not a claim to replace production infrastructure. It is a concrete system in which a reader can trace accepted work through actual C++ code, sockets, SQLite transactions, retries, and process tests, then identify exactly what a larger deployment would have to add.

Carry that discipline into the next design. Choose the authority, state the invariant, bound the resource, define the failure history, and retain evidence. When a framework or optimization is introduced, ask which assumption it replaces and how the replacement will be verified. That is the continuity between professional C++ programming and dependable distributed systems.
